newsitem.title: USA: FORECAST--U.S. May CPI to show inflation tame.
newsitem.headline: FORECAST--U.S. May CPI to show inflation tame.

text.p: The May Consumer Price Index (CPI) set for release on Tuesday, June 17, is expected to provide yet more evidence of low inflation and further assure the market that the Federal Reserve will not raise interest rates in July, economists said.

The May CPI is expected to be up 0.2 percent, after rising 0.1 percent in April, according to economists polled by Reuters on Friday. The core CPI, the index without its more volatile food and energy components, is also expected to be up 0.2 percent after rising 0.3 percent in April.
Food prices trends were mixed in May, said Daiwa Securities America chief economist Michael Moran. Among items in the core index, Moran said airline fares might be up again.
"We think they could show a rather large increase," he said. "And medical costs are rising a little bit faster than they did last year and in the early part of this year."

Charles Lieberman, chief economist at Chase Securities Inc, said he, too, looks for small changes in the May CPI. He expects the overall CPI to be flat after rising 0.1 percent in April. And he looks for a 0.1 percent rise in the core CPI.
"Apparel and tobacco prices were up in April and we expect them to be weaker this month," said Lieberman. "Energy prices will be down, though, and that's why we expect the total CPI to be flat."
Peter D'Antonio, senior economist at Citicorp Global Finance N.A., looks for a 0.1 percent rise in the CPI overall and a 0.2 percent increase in the core CPI.
"Energy will be a little lower because gasoline prices have fallen," he said.
D'Antonio said the May CPI data will offer more evidence of low inflation.
"Inflation is running at about 2.5 percent so far this year and I would not look for any pick-up as you go through the year," D'Antonio said.
Seen in the context of five consecutive months of declines in wholesale price inflation, D'Antonio said, "There's just no inflation to worry about at this point."
One question is whether the financial markets can get any more mileage out of good inflation news or whether by now, good news is no news.

"What you may see happening as more reports of low inflation or weak economic growth come in for the second quarter is that the market will react less and less," said Joshua Feinman, vice president and global markets economist at Bankers Trust. "The data have taken the Fed out for July. But now we've done that trade," he said.

"We're at 6.72 percent on the bond (yield) and 6.03 percent on the two-year note (yield)," said Feinman. "From here, you have to answer the question as to what will happen in the second half of the year.
